[[File:Texas mountain laurel fruiting stage.jpg|thumb|A specimen of ''Dermatophyllum secundiflorum'' in its fruiting stage.]]
'''''Dermatophyllum secundiflorum''''' is a species of [[Flowering plant|flowering]] [[shrub]] or small tree in the family [[Fabaceae]]<ref name="USFS">{{cite web |url=http://www.fs.fed.us/database/feis/plants/tree/sopsec/all.html |title=Sophora secundiflora |first=Ronald J. |last=Uchytil |work=Fire Effects Information System |publisher=United States Forest Service |year=1990 |access-date=2009-12-29}}</ref> that is native to the [[Southwestern United States]] ([[Texas]], [[New Mexico]]) and Mexico ([[Chihuahua (state)|Chihuahua]] and [[Coahuila]] south to [[Hidalgo (Mexico)|Hidalgo]], [[Puebla]], and [[Querétaro]]).<ref>{{GRIN | accessdate=2009-12-29}}</ref> Its common names include '''Texas mountain laurel''', '''Texas mescalbean''', '''grape Koolaid tree,''' '''''frijolito''''', and '''''frijolillo'''''.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-04-20 |title=Texas Mountain Laurel: Fragrant Native Tree for the South |url=https://theplantnative.com/plant/texas-mountain-laurel/ |access-date=2026-07-26 |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name="USFS"/> 

==Name==
Although "mescalbean" is among the plant's common monikers, it bears no relation to the ''[[Agave]]'' species used to make the spirit [[mezcal]], nor to the [[peyote]] cactus (''Lophophora williamsii''), which contains the hallucinogenic alkaloid [[mescaline]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://waynesword.palomar.edu/peyote.htm |title=Mescal Bean & The Unrelated Peyote Cactus |work=Plants That Make You Loco |publisher=Wayne's World |access-date=2009-12-29 |archive-date=2010-01-14 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100114151034/http://waynesword.palomar.edu/peyote.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref> The common name "Texas mountain laurel" is also misleading, as it is unrelated to true [[Kalmia latifolia|mountain laurel]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://texastreeid.tamu.edu/content/TreeDetails/?id=120 |title=Mescalbean|publisher=Texas A&M Forest Service|accessdate=2024-01-16 }}</ref>

==Description==
An [[evergreen]], this small tree's [[Leaf|leaves]] are [[pinnate]]ly compound, with small, roughly spatulate [[leaflet (botany)|leaflets]]. The leaflets are thick, and waxy to the touch. Rarely having a single, straight trunk, its [[Bark (botany)|bark]] is smooth in all but the oldest specimens.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://ag.arizona.edu/pima/gardening/aridplants/Sophora_secundiflora.html |title=Sophora secundiflora Texas mountain laurel |work=Arid Plant List |publisher=Pima County Home Horticulture |date=2004-05-16 |access-date=2009-12-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100228043413/http://ag.arizona.edu/pima/gardening/aridplants/Sophora_secundiflora.html |archive-date=2010-02-28 |url-status=dead }}</ref> It grows slowly to a height of {{convert|15|ft|m|abbr=on}} and has a crown diameter of {{convert|10|ft|m|abbr=on}}.<ref name="Mielke">{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7KFT2hGIFPMC |title=Native Plants for Southwestern Landscapes |first=Judy |last=Mielke |publisher=University of Texas Press |year=1993 |isbn=978-0-292-75147-7|page=258}}</ref>

Extremely fragrant purple [[flower]]s, resembling the smell of [[grape soda]], are produced in large clusters in March and April.<ref name=":0">{{Cite news|url=https://www.sacbee.com/entertainment/living/home-garden/article22481463.html|title=Arboretum Spotlight: Smell the grape soda|work=The Sacramento Bee|access-date=2019-05-14|language=en-US|issn=0890-5738}}</ref> They are followed by {{convert|4|in|cm|abbr=on}} [[Legume|pods]] containing dark or bright orange or red [[seed]]s.<ref name="Mielke"/>

==Habitat==
It is well-adapted to [[arid]] and [[Semi-arid climate|semiarid]] habitats, but is most common in [[riparian zone]]s.<ref name="USFS"/>

==Uses==
''D. secundiflorum'' is a popular [[ornamental plant]] due to its showy [[flower]]s and orange [[seed]]s. The reddish [[wood]] that it produces is potentially useful, but as yet has little commercial value.

The seeds were once used by some [[Indigenous peoples of the Americas|Native American]] tribes as a [[recreational drug]], before being supplanted by [[peyote]]{{citation needed|date=August 2026}}. This plant is psychoactive but is also extremely toxic due to the presence of the bicyclic [[alkaloid]] [[cytisine]], which is chemically related to [[nicotine]].<ref name=":0" />  The consumption of a single seed is enough to kill an adult.<ref>{{cite book |last=Little |first=Elbert L. |title=The Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Trees: Western Region |year=1994 |orig-year=1980 |publisher=Knopf |isbn=0394507614 |edition=Chanticleer Press|page=506}}</ref>
